newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-NEW ZEALAND END TRIUMPHANT YEAR WITH FLOURISH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-NEW ZEALAND END TRIUMPHANT YEAR WITH FLOURISH.

text.p: Words spoke almost as loudly as deeds at rugby union's world headquarters last Saturday.
Before a capacity Twickenham audience, the New Zealand Barbarians dazzled at the expense of the full England side in a glimpse of the kind of rugby needed to win the 1999 World Cup.
England, despite some promising moments in a 34-19 defeat, were as predictable as their coach Jack Rowell at the post-match news conference.

In language beloved of corporate middle managers everywhere, Rowell spoke of a playing schedule more "interactive with the southern hemisphere". In even more tortured syntax, he also refered to something called "systematic continuity skills".
All Black coach John Hart, by contrast, was refreshingly direct.
Pace, Hart, said was the main difference between the two teams.
"One of the decisive factors was speed," he said. "Ultimately the game at pace got to England and we kept playing at pace.
"Under the new rules speed is a very important ingredient of the game. Size is okay, but we need skill and strength, that's the modern game."
Two examples late in the match showed how swiftly New Zealand have adapted to the new rules.

The final try from Joeli Vidiri came as a result of a swift interchange between locks Ian Jones and Robin Brooke, standing in the backline, a move identified by Hart as an example of the all-round skills needed by all players in the modern age.
The other was the substitution of fly-half Andrew Mehrtens after 60 minutes by the remarkable young talent of Carlos Spencer, who kicked two penalties and scored a wonderful solo try.
Hart is already exploring the possibilities allowed by tactical substitutions, also replacing number eight Taine Randall by Mika Dylan, who made a significant impact late in the match.
"With the intensity of rugby we need all the backup we can get," he said.

England, with nothing to lose in a non-international match, made no substitutions, although it might have been a kindness to let scrum-half Andy Gomarsall take an early bath after a distinctly mixed display.
The match finished a triumphant year for New Zealand under their evergreen captain Sean Fitzpatrick.

The All Blacks won the first Tri-Nations series against world champions South Africa and Australia, took their first ever series in South Africa and thumped Scotland for good measure in a two-match series.
"They're definitely the best team in the world at the moment," acknowledged England pack leader Jason Leonard.
"It was a great way to finish our '96 season for New Zealand rugby," Hart said.
Fitzpatrick added: "The way we have played this year is the way we have played today.
"It's wonderful to finish the season on a high. I saw in the last 10 minutes the guys really wanted to win."
